lesson.title: Molecular Clocks: Reading Evolutionary Time in DNA
lesson.summary: Molecular clocks use the steady accumulation of mutations in DNA or protein sequences to estimate how long ago two lineages diverged from a shared ancestor, producing a dated estimate rather than an exact number.
lesson.body:
You already know that similarities in DNA and protein sequences are strong evidence that species share a common ancestor, and that phylogenetics uses those similarities to build cladograms showing which lineages branched off from which. A cladogram on its own tells you the order in which branching happened, but not when. Molecular clocks add that missing dimension of time.

The basic idea rests on a simple observation: mutations accumulate in a lineage's DNA over generations. Many of these mutations are neutral, meaning they neither help nor hurt an organism's survival or reproduction, so natural selection does not strongly filter them out or favor them. Because neutral mutations build up more or less steadily over time, the number of sequence differences between two living species gives a rough measure of how much time has passed since they last shared a common ancestor. Two species with many sequence differences in a given gene are inferred to have diverged longer ago than two species with only a few differences.

A molecular clock by itself only gives relative time, so it has to be calibrated against something with a known age, usually a well dated fossil. If paleontologists know that two lineages had already split by a certain point in the fossil record, that date anchors the clock and lets biologists convert "number of sequence differences" into an estimate of "millions of years." Because mutation rates are not perfectly constant across all genes or all lineages (they can be affected by generation time, metabolic rate, and other factors), scientists typically check estimates using multiple genes and multiple calibration points, then report the divergence time as a range rather than a single fixed number.

This is worth stating plainly: molecular clock dates are estimates with real uncertainty, not exact measurements like reading a calendar. A frequently cited example is the divergence of the human and chimpanzee lineages, which molecular clock studies place at roughly 5 to 7 million years ago. Different genes and different studies produce somewhat different numbers within that range, which is exactly what you would expect from a method that depends on assumptions about mutation rate and calibration accuracy, not a flaw that undermines the whole approach.

When a molecular clock estimate is layered onto a cladogram, the result is a dated phylogeny: a branching diagram where the branch points are labeled with estimated ages. That combination, sequence comparison for relationships plus molecular clock for timing, is one of the main ways biologists reconstruct the timeline of life, from when major animal groups split apart to when a particular species is thought to have evolved.
